title: Structural Design Patterns
summary: Seven ways to compose objects and classes into bigger structures — Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge, and Flyweight.

blocks.markdown:
**Structural patterns** describe how to compose classes and objects into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient.

- Creational patterns handle **how objects get made**; structural patterns handle **how objects fit together**.
- Most work by **wrapping** or **combining** existing objects instead of inheriting from them.
- The GoF lists seven: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge, Flyweight.
- Interviews probe these constantly — they show up in real LLD questions (parking lots, file systems, payment gateways).

blocks.subTitle: The seven at a glance
blocks.markdown:
One line per pattern.

| Pattern | Solves |
|---|---|
| Adapter | Mismatched interfaces |
| Decorator | Add behavior at runtime |
| Facade | Simplify a complex subsystem |
| Proxy | Control access to an object |
| Composite | Treat a tree uniformly |
| Bridge | Split abstraction from implementation |
| Flyweight | Share state to cut memory |

See [design-patterns-overview](design-patterns-overview) for how these relate to creational and behavioral patterns.

**Adapter** converts the interface of an existing class into another interface a client expects, without changing the original class.

- Problem: you have a working class, but its method names/signatures don't match what your code calls.
- Use when integrating a **third-party library** or **legacy code** you can't modify.
- The adapter wraps the old object and translates calls — a thin **translation layer**, nothing more.
- Real example: plugging a `LegacyLogger.write(msg)` into code expecting a `Logger.log(msg)` interface.

blocks.markdown:
**Decorator** attaches new behavior to an object at runtime by wrapping it in another object with the same interface.

- Problem: you need optional, combinable extras (e.g. compression, encryption) without a subclass for every combination.
- Each decorator holds a reference to the wrapped object and **adds work before/after** delegating to it.
- Decorators can **stack** — wrap a decorator in another decorator.
- Real example: `Coffee` → `MilkDecorator(Coffee)` → `SugarDecorator(MilkDecorator(Coffee))`.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
interface Coffee:
    method cost()

class SimpleCoffee implements Coffee:
    method cost():
        return 50

// base decorator holds the wrapped Coffee, same interface
abstract class CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee:
    field wrapped: Coffee

    constructor(coffee):
        this.wrapped = coffee

class MilkDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator:
    method cost():
        return this.wrapped.cost() + 10   // add behavior, then delegate

class SugarDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator:
    method cost():
        return this.wrapped.cost() + 5

// stack decorators freely, at runtime
order = new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new SimpleCoffee()))
print(order.cost())   // 65
```

**Facade** provides a single, simplified interface in front of a complex subsystem of many classes.

- Problem: clients need to call several subsystem classes in a precise order just to do one task.
- The facade doesn't add new logic — it just **coordinates existing classes** behind one clean method.
- Subsystem classes stay usable directly for callers who need fine control.
- Real example: `startComputer()` on a facade internally calls `cpu.boot()`, `memory.load()`, `disk.spinUp()`.

blocks.markdown:
**Proxy** provides a stand-in object that controls access to a real object, matching its interface exactly.

- Problem: you need to add a check or optimization **before** reaching the real object — without the client knowing.
- Common kinds: **virtual proxy** (delay creating an expensive object until needed), **protection proxy** (check permissions), **remote proxy** (stand in for an object on another machine).
- Unlike a decorator, a proxy usually controls **whether/when** the call reaches the real object, not just what happens around it.
- Real example: an `ImageProxy` that loads the real image file only on first `display()` call.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
interface Image:
    method display()

// expensive real object
class RealImage implements Image:
    field filename

    constructor(filename):
        this.filename = filename
        this.loadFromDisk()   // costly

    method loadFromDisk():
        print("loading " + this.filename)

    method display():
        print("showing " + this.filename)

// proxy matches the interface, controls access/timing
class ImageProxy implements Image:
    field filename
    field real = null

    constructor(filename):
        this.filename = filename

    method display():
        if this.real == null:
            this.real = new RealImage(this.filename)   // create lazily
        this.real.display()

image = new ImageProxy("diagram.png")   // no load yet
image.display()                          // loads now, then shows
```

**Composite** lets you compose objects into tree structures and treat a single object and a group of objects **the same way**.

- Problem: code has to keep checking "is this a single item or a group?" before acting on it.
- Both leaves (single items) and composites (containers) implement the **same interface**, so client code calls one method regardless of which it holds.
- A composite's method typically just **loops over its children** and calls the same method on each.
- Real example: a file system where `File` and `Folder` both implement `getSize()`.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
interface FileSystemNode:
    method getSize()

// leaf — no children
class File implements FileSystemNode:
    field size

    constructor(size):
        this.size = size

    method getSize():
        return this.size

// composite — holds children, same interface as a leaf
class Folder implements FileSystemNode:
    field children = []

    method add(node: FileSystemNode):
        this.children.append(node)

    method getSize():
        total = 0
        for child in this.children:
            total = total + child.getSize()   // works for File or Folder
        return total

root = new Folder()
root.add(new File(100))
sub = new Folder()
sub.add(new File(50))
root.add(sub)
print(root.getSize())   // 150, no type-checking needed
```

**Bridge** splits a class into two independent hierarchies — an **abstraction** and an **implementation** — connected by composition instead of inheritance.

- Problem: a class hierarchy grows two ways at once (e.g. shape type × rendering method), causing a subclass explosion (`CircleOpenGL`, `CircleDirectX`, `SquareOpenGL`...).
- The abstraction (`Shape`) holds a reference to an implementation interface (`Renderer`) rather than inheriting it.
- Either side can now change or grow **independently** — new shapes or new renderers don't multiply classes.
- Real example: `RemoteControl` (abstraction) working with any `Device` (implementation) — TV or radio.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
// implementation hierarchy — "how" to render
interface Renderer:
    method renderCircle(radius)

class OpenGLRenderer implements Renderer:
    method renderCircle(radius):
        print("OpenGL circle r=" + radius)

class DirectXRenderer implements Renderer:
    method renderCircle(radius):
        print("DirectX circle r=" + radius)

// abstraction hierarchy — "what" to draw, holds a Renderer
abstract class Shape:
    field renderer: Renderer

    constructor(renderer):
        this.renderer = renderer

    abstract method draw()

class Circle extends Shape:
    field radius

    constructor(renderer, radius):
        super(renderer)
        this.radius = radius

    method draw():
        this.renderer.renderCircle(this.radius)   // delegate to implementation side

// mix any shape with any renderer, independently
circle = new Circle(new OpenGLRenderer(), 5)
circle.draw()
```

**Flyweight** cuts memory use by sharing one object across many contexts instead of creating a duplicate for each.

- Problem: you need huge numbers of similar objects (characters in a document, trees in a forest) and per-object memory adds up fast.
- Split state into **intrinsic** (shared, unchanging — a character's glyph shape) and **extrinsic** (unique per use, passed in — its position on the page).
- A **factory** hands out existing shared instances instead of `new`-ing duplicates.
- Real example: a text editor storing one `CharacterGlyph` per letter, reused at thousands of positions.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
// flyweight — holds only intrinsic (shared) state
class CharacterGlyph:
    field character
    field font

    constructor(character, font):
        this.character = character
        this.font = font

    method render(x, y):        // extrinsic state passed in per call
        print(this.character + " at (" + x + "," + y + ")")

// factory caches and reuses flyweights by key
class GlyphFactory:
    field cache = {}

    method getGlyph(character, font):
        key = character + font
        if key not in this.cache:
            this.cache[key] = new CharacterGlyph(character, font)   // create once
        return this.cache[key]

factory = new GlyphFactory()
// 3 positions, but only 1 'A' glyph object is ever created
factory.getGlyph("A", "Arial").render(0, 0)
factory.getGlyph("A", "Arial").render(10, 0)
factory.getGlyph("A", "Arial").render(20, 0)
```

blocks.subTitle: Decorator vs Proxy vs Adapter
blocks.markdown:
All three wrap an object behind the same-ish interface — the intent differs.

| Pattern | Intent |
|---|---|
| Adapter | Fix a mismatched interface |
| Decorator | Add behavior, stays optional/stackable |
| Proxy | Control or delay access to the real object |

Adapter changes the **interface shape**; Decorator and Proxy keep the same interface but change **what happens** when it's called.

Common mistakes:

- **"Decorator and inheritance are interchangeable."** Inheritance fixes behavior at compile time and multiplies subclasses for combinations; Decorator composes at runtime and stacks freely.
- **"Proxy and Decorator are the same because both wrap objects."** Proxy controls *access* (may skip the real call entirely); Decorator always delegates and *adds* to it.
- **Overusing Facade to hide bad design.** A facade that clients bypass constantly is a sign the subsystem itself needs fixing, not just hiding.

blocks.subTitle: Adapter vs Facade
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Adapter vs Facade — how are they different?**

Both wrap something, but for different reasons. **Adapter** converts one interface into another so incompatible code can work together — it's about *translation*. **Facade** simplifies access to a complex subsystem by exposing one clean method — it's about *convenience*. An adapter typically wraps one class; a facade typically coordinates many.

blocks.subTitle: Decorator vs inheritance
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why use Decorator instead of just subclassing?**

Subclassing fixes each combination as its own class — `MilkCoffee`, `SugarCoffee`, `MilkSugarCoffee` — which explodes as options grow, and it's fixed at compile time. Decorator wraps objects at runtime, so you combine behaviors freely (`new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(coffee))`) without a class per combination.

blocks.subTitle: Proxy vs Decorator confusion
blocks.markdown:
**Q: If both Proxy and Decorator wrap an object with the same interface, what's actually different?**

Intent. **Proxy** controls access — it may lazy-load, check permissions, or forward to a remote object, and can refuse or delay the real call. **Decorator** always calls through and layers extra behavior on top. In code they can look identical; the difference is *why* the wrapper exists.

blocks.subTitle: When to use Composite
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would you reach for Composite?**

When you have a part-whole tree and client code keeps branching on "is this a leaf or a container?" Composite gives leaves and containers the same interface, so a method like `getSize()` or `render()` works uniformly at any level — file systems, UI component trees, org charts.

blocks.subTitle: What problem Flyweight solves
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What problem does Flyweight actually solve, and what's the catch?**

It cuts memory when you need massive numbers of similar objects, by sharing the unchanging (**intrinsic**) part and passing the per-use (**extrinsic**) part in on each call. The catch: it adds complexity (a factory, a cache) and only pays off at real scale — using it for a handful of objects is premature optimization.

blocks.subTitle: Bridge vs Adapter
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Bridge and Adapter both use composition to connect interfaces — what's the real difference?**

**Adapter** is applied *after the fact* to make an existing, incompatible class fit — a retrofit. **Bridge** is designed *upfront* to keep an abstraction and its implementation separate from the start, so both can evolve independently. Adapter fixes a mismatch; Bridge prevents one.
